# Vīmaṁsaka Sutta (MN 47 (PTS MN i 317))

**ID:** MN 47 (PTS MN i 317)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Vīmaṁsaka Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 317

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vīmaṁsaka Sutta* ("The Inquirer", MN 47; PTS MN i 317) is the forty-seventh discourse of the Majjhimanikāya [Anālayo; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, the sutta addresses the procedure of inquiry to be undertaken by a prospective disciple [Anālayo; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. In contrast to traditional Indian conceptions of teacher authority that could not be questioned, the Buddha encourages the mendicants to make a thorough investigation of himself to determine whether his claim to full awakening is justified [Anālayo; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. He outlines specific criteria for scrutiny—examining bodily and verbal behaviors over time to ascertain whether defiled or mixed states are present—so that faith in the Tathāgata is established as reasoned, grounded on direct observation (*ākāravatī saddhā dassanamūlikā daḷhā*), rather than blind belief [Anālayo; Lin 2015; Rogell 2003; Nyanaponika & Fromm 1986].

The discourse has a direct parallel in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 186), translated by Gautama Saṅghadeva in the late fourth century CE from an Indian Prākrit original transmitted in the Sarvāstivāda tradition [Anālayo]. A passage on grounded faith from the sutta (MN i 320) is also cited in Harivarman's *Tattvasiddhi* [Lin 2015].
